metadata.title: Same Prompt, Different Answer
metadata.audience: anyone shipping on an LLM who has filed a bug report about inconsistent output
metadata.greeting_note: hello lexicon: Portuguese, one word. Not reused — prior: Hola/Jambo, Ciao/Hej, Sawubona/Merhaba, Namaste, Bonjour, Annyeong.
metadata.note: Track ai-. Every probability, percentage and float on screen is computed by sampling_evidence.py, which ships here — no model is called and nothing is measured from a live system. The logits are illustrative and the reel says so; the ARGUMENT is about the shape of the softmax, which holds for any logits. The temperature-0 section claims only what the script shows plus what SGLang's own docs state; it does NOT claim a measured rate of divergence for any real model. Outro is HaiTitleOutro. B02 uses ClaudeBarChart, NOT BarChart: the latter imports the vox token set (flat white ground, accent defined as plain ink) and renders a Claude reel off-brand with no terracotta. Caught on frame review 2026-10-16.

skin_warnings: B08: palette=claude but the outro is 'HaiTitleOutro' — OUTRO LAW wants ClaudeTitleOutro

beats.narration_text: Olá. This is Jainil. You send the same prompt twice and get two different answers, so you file it as a bug. It usually is not one. There is a specific place the difference comes from, and a second place that surprises people even after they have turned the temperature down to zero.

show.event: composer on cream, spark + 'Olá, Jainil' above it
the question types itself in
send arms terracotta, running indicator
two output lines land

props.command: Same prompt, same model, two different answers. Is this a bug?
output: And temperature 0 won't fix it either.

beats.narration_text: Here is the whole idea in one breath. The model does not pick a word. It produces a probability for every word it could say next, and then something draws one. Temperature does not add the randomness — it decides how peaked that distribution is before the draw happens.

show.event: empty cream page, caret blinking
writer types 'The model picks the next word.'
writer stops on 'picks', deletes it
'draws' types in its place

props.text:
The model picks
the next word.

beats.narration_text: This is one position in one answer. Seven candidate words, and the probability the model assigns to each. The most likely word, the, gets forty-six and a half percent. Which means that at this one position, better than half the time, you get something that is not the. Nothing has gone wrong. That is the distribution doing exactly what it says.

show.event: title, then bars grow in order as the voice names the candidates
the tallest bar, 'the', lights terracotta at 46.5%
the remaining six bars sit visibly under it

beats.narration_text: Now turn the temperature down to nought point two. Same model, same scores, same position — but the shape changes. The dashed outline is where we just were. The solid shape is the same distribution at the lower temperature: the top word now takes ninety-five percent and everything else is flattened into the floor. Lower temperature does not mean more correct. It means more peaked.

show.event: the temperature-1.0 shape appears first as a dashed ghost
the temperature-0.2 shape draws solid over it — a spike
the collapse of the other six candidates is plain
caption lands

props.title: THE SAME SCORES AT TEMPERATURE 0.2
props.caption: Dashed is T=1.0. Temperature reshapes the distribution; it does not add noise.

beats.narration_text: And here is why even a low temperature does not buy you a repeatable answer. This is the chance that every single token in an answer takes the top choice, plotted against how long the answer is, at temperature nought point two. One token, ninety-five percent. Ten tokens, sixty percent. Fifty tokens, eight percent. Two hundred tokens — one in twenty-three thousand.

show.event: axes draw, curve starts high on the left at 95%
it falls away through 60% and 28%
it reaches the floor at 200 tokens
the low point lights terracotta with the odds

props.title: CHANCE OF THE IDENTICAL ANSWER, AT T=0.2
props.caption: Even at a low temperature, two identical long answers are a coincidence.

beats.narration_text: So you set temperature to zero. Now it takes the highest score every time — no draw at all. And it still varies. Here is why. These are the same thousand numbers added up twice: once one at a time, once in ten blocks. Floating point addition is not associative, so the order changes the answer. Look where they stop agreeing.

show.event: the first sum types in, in mono
the second sum lands beneath it, character-aligned
everything from the first disagreeing digit turns terracotta on both rows
the size of the gap lands beneath

props.title: THE SAME THOUSAND NUMBERS
props.caption: Same inputs. Different order of addition. Different result.

beats.narration_text: Be careful with that, though. Non-associativity on its own does not make a model unpredictable — the same code on the same input in the same order gives the same answer every time. What changes the order is dynamic batching. Your request lands in a batch of a different size, the kernel splits its sums differently, and the scores shift by a hair. This is from SGLang's own documentation.

show.event: cream card, the quote reveals line by line
citation settles beneath, smaller and softer

lines: “The main source is varying batch sizes. Different batch sizes cause GPU kernels to split reduction operations differently, leading to different addition orders.”
“Even with temperature=0, standard LLM inference can produce different outputs due to dynamic batching.”

beats.narration_text: Your turn. If you have ever written a test that asserts an exact model output, try this one: I have tests that compare model output to an expected string, and they fail intermittently. Help me rewrite them to assert on the properties I actually care about instead of on exact text. That is the fix. Not a lower temperature.

show.event: composer again, greeting reads 'Your turn.'
the viewer's prompt types itself in full
send arms terracotta and holds
